newsitem.title: INDIA: Chinese entrepreneurs seek soymeal from India.
newsitem.headline: Chinese entrepreneurs seek soymeal from India.

text.p: Chinese businessmen, visiting India to seek out business opportunities, said on Thursday they were keen to source soymeal, rice and other foodgrains from India.
"Over the last five days we have booked over 20,000 metric tonnes of soymeal from India," said Liu Yonghao, chairman of the Hope Group, China's largest private enterprise.
Yonghao said his company's annual consumption of soymeal was about 300,000 metric tonnes.

"The rapidly improving living conditions in China have seen soymeal consumption going up," Yonghao said. "How much we take from India depends on the price and quality. It will vary from time to time."
Yonghao, who gave up a teaching job to set up his firm in 1982 with a $200 stake after selling his wristwatch and bicycle, said his group's turnover last year was $400 million.
"The process of development of my own company is illustrative of the development of the Chinese private sector," Yonghao said.
China's GNP, which has grown 9.5 percent each year since economic reforms were launched in 1979, is estimated to rise by 10 percent in 1996, officials said.
"We are trying to grasp all opportunities that may prove useful to us," he added. "If your policy permits, we can also look into real estate development."

Xiu Lirong, the chairwoman of the Dunhuang Group, which has interests ranging from textiles to real estate and an annual turnover of more than $20 million last year, also said she hoped to tie up deals for the import of rice and soymeal.
"I have met some firms and we will decide once we receive their quotations," she said.
Yonghao and Lirong were part of a 14-member delegation of the All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce, China's biggest confederation of industry, which is visiting India.
"Bilateral trade between India and China is presently just 0.04 percent of total Chinese foreign trade," said Zhang Xuwu, the leader of the delegation.
Trade between the two countries stood at $1.2 billion last year, Zhuwu said.
"That is not commensurate with the size and population of our two countries. We want to raise it to $12 billion, but that is still very small."
